title: Clostridioides difficile infection in a surgical patient

guidelineVersions: NICE NG199 (published 23 July 2021; current version dated 11 July 2024)

brief.scenario: Mrs Laura Penrose, 73, has new frequent watery diarrhoea after a course of antibiotics.
brief.task: Assess suspected Clostridioides difficile infection and outline immediate management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Assess severity and complications first; stop what's unnecessary; treat according to guidance; never reach for loperamide.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Reaching for an antimotility drug, or continuing the causative antibiotic without review.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess her ABCDE and hydration, then take a focused history of the diarrhoea and her recent antibiotics."

grid.label: Initial assessment
grid.fail: Does not assess ABCDE or hydration before focusing only on the diarrhoea.
grid.pass: Assesses ABCDE and hydration status alongside the history.
grid.high: Links dehydration and electrolyte disturbance explicitly to the risk of deterioration in an older patient.

grid.label: Focused history
grid.fail: Does not ask about antibiotic exposure or previous C. difficile.
grid.pass: Asks about onset, stool frequency, abdominal pain, fever, previous C. difficile, and reviews recent antibiotics, hospital exposure, laxatives and other medicines.
grid.high: Specifically identifies which antibiotic is the likely trigger and whether it, or any other non-essential medicine, can be stopped.

grid.label: Examination for complications
grid.fail: Does not examine for distension, tenderness, ileus, toxic megacolon or peritonitis.
grid.pass: Assesses for abdominal distension, tenderness, ileus, toxic megacolon or peritonitis.
grid.high: Explains that a rigid or silent abdomen in this context changes management from ward-based treatment to urgent surgical involvement.

grid.label: Isolation and antibiotic stewardship
grid.fail: Continues the triggering antibiotic without review, and does not isolate the patient.
grid.pass: Isolates according to infection-control precautions, stops unnecessary antibiotics and checks whether an essential antibiotic could be changed to one with lower C. difficile risk.
grid.high: Records the diagnosis clearly for future antibiotic decisions and considers PPIs, laxatives and other medicines that could be worsening diarrhoea or dehydration.

grid.label: Safe symptomatic management
grid.fail: Prescribes loperamide or another antimotility drug for the diarrhoea.
grid.pass: Does not offer antimotility medicines such as loperamide in suspected or confirmed C. difficile infection.
grid.high: Explains the mechanism: slowing transit keeps toxin in contact with the bowel for longer and can worsen the illness.

grid.label: First-line treatment
grid.fail: Treats all diarrhoea as C. difficile without stool confirmation, or gives an outdated or unsupported treatment.
grid.pass: Obtains stool testing via the local diagnostic pathway and treats confirmed or strongly suspected infection according to current NICE guidance.
grid.high: Names oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days as first-line for a first episode, with fidaxomicin as an alternative if vancomycin is ineffective.

grid.label: Recognising when to escalate
grid.fail: Manages severe deterioration, ileus, toxic megacolon or peritonitis without escalating.
grid.pass: Seeks urgent specialist or surgical advice for severe deterioration, ileus, toxic megacolon, perforation or life-threatening infection.
grid.high: Also flags recurrent infection as a separate problem needing its own management plan and involves microbiology or gastroenterology proactively.

failures.consequence: Toxin stays in contact with the bowel for longer, worsening the infection.

failures.move: Continuing the triggering antibiotic without review.
failures.consequence: The infection is perpetuated instead of settling.

failures.move: Treating all diarrhoea as C. difficile, or using an outdated treatment.
Continuing ward-based management despite abdominal distension and silence.
failures.consequence: Delayed recognition of toxic megacolon or perforation.

failures.move: Not examining for peritonism or distension.
failures.consequence: A surgical complication is missed until it is advanced.

recovery.when: Pushed to give loperamide for comfort
recovery.line: I'd still avoid antimotility drugs here, because they can worsen suspected C. difficile infection.

recovery.when: Asked why you'd stop the antibiotic
recovery.line: I'd still want to stop it unless it's essential, because ongoing exposure perpetuates the infection.

knowledge.fact: Do not offer antimotility medicines such as loperamide in suspected or confirmed C. difficile infection.
Review existing antibiotics and stop unless essential; if essential, consider switching to lower-risk options.
First-line treatment for a first episode in adults is oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days; fidaxomicin is an alternative if vancomycin fails.
Toxic megacolon, ileus, perforation or peritonitis need urgent specialist or surgical advice.

recall.think: Toxic megacolon or perforation behind what looks like simple diarrhoea.
recall.say: "I'd stop unnecessary antibiotics, avoid antimotility drugs, and treat according to current NICE guidance."
do: Stop/review causative antibiotic and other contributing medicines

push.question: Would you give loperamide while you wait for the stool result?
push.expect: No — antimotility drugs are not recommended in suspected C. difficile.

push.question: What antibiotics would you stop?
push.expect: Review and stop unnecessary antibiotics; consider switching an essential one to lower-risk.

push.question: What treatment would you start once confirmed?
push.expect: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days first-line; fidaxomicin if that fails.

push.question: Her abdomen becomes distended and bowel sounds disappear. What now?
push.expect: Urgent specialist/surgical advice for possible toxic megacolon or ileus.

curveballs.prompt: "She's uncomfortable, can we just give loperamide?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — it risks worsening the infection by keeping toxin in contact with the bowel.

curveballs.prompt: "It's just diarrhoea, does the antibiotic really need stopping?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes, unless essential — ongoing exposure perpetuates the infection.

curveballs.prompt: The nurse says the abdomen is now silent and distended.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Treat as a possible toxic megacolon and get urgent surgical/specialist advice.
